subtopics.title: 6.1 Waves in air, fluids and solids

questions.subtopic: 6.1 Waves in air, fluids and solids
questions.sourceSubtopic: 6.1 Waves in air, fluids and solids
questions.question: Distinguish transverse and longitudinal waves and give an example of each.
questions.modelAnswer: Transverse oscillations are perpendicular to energy transfer, e.g. electromagnetic or water-surface waves. Longitudinal oscillations are parallel, e.g. sound waves.
markingPoints: Transverse oscillations are perpendicular to energy transfer, e.g. electromagnetic or water-surface waves.
Longitudinal oscillations are parallel, e.g. sound waves.

questions.subtopic: 6.1 Waves in air, fluids and solids
questions.sourceSubtopic: 6.1 Waves in air, fluids and solids
questions.question: Define amplitude, wavelength, frequency and period.
questions.modelAnswer: Amplitude: maximum displacement from equilibrium. Wavelength: distance between corresponding points on adjacent waves. Frequency: waves passing a point per second. Period: time for one complete wave.
markingPoints: Wavelength: distance between corresponding points on adjacent waves.
Frequency: waves passing a point per second.
Period: time for one complete wave.

questions.subtopic: 6.1 Waves in air, fluids and solids
questions.sourceSubtopic: 6.1 Waves in air, fluids and solids
questions.question: What do waves transfer?
questions.modelAnswer: Energy and information. Waves do not cause an overall transfer of matter.
markingPoints: Waves do not cause an overall transfer of matter.

questions.subtopic: 6.1 Waves in air, fluids and solids
questions.sourceSubtopic: 6.1 Waves in air, fluids and solids
questions.question: State the law of reflection.
questions.modelAnswer: Angle of incidence equals angle of reflection. Angles are measured from the normal.
markingPoints: Angle of incidence equals angle of reflection.
Angles are measured from the normal.

questions.subtopic: 6.1 Waves in air, fluids and solids
questions.sourceSubtopic: 6.1 Waves in air, fluids and solids
questions.question: Explain why a wave changes direction when it enters a different medium at an angle.
questions.modelAnswer: Wave speed changes at the boundary. One side of the wavefront changes speed first. The wavefront pivots. Frequency stays constant while wavelength changes.
markingPoints: Wave speed changes at the boundary.
One side of the wavefront changes speed first.
Frequency stays constant while wavelength changes.

questions.subtopic: 6.1 Waves in air, fluids and solids
questions.sourceSubtopic: 6.1 Waves in air, fluids and solids
questions.question: Explain how sound travels through air.
questions.modelAnswer: A vibrating source produces compressions and rarefactions. Air particles oscillate parallel to energy transfer. Neighbouring particles pass on the disturbance.
markingPoints: A vibrating source produces compressions and rarefactions.
Air particles oscillate parallel to energy transfer.
Neighbouring particles pass on the disturbance.

questions.subtopic: 6.1 Waves in air, fluids and solids
questions.sourceSubtopic: 6.1 Waves in air, fluids and solids
questions.question: Give two uses of ultrasound and explain the measurement principle.
questions.modelAnswer: Examples: medical imaging and sonar. A pulse is transmitted and reflected at a boundary. Time delay and wave speed are used to calculate distance, often distance = speed × time ÷ 2.
markingPoints: A pulse is transmitted and reflected at a boundary.
Time delay and wave speed are used to calculate distance, often distance = speed × time ÷ 2.

questions.subtopic: 6.2 Electromagnetic waves
questions.sourceSubtopic: 6.2 Electromagnetic waves
questions.question: List the electromagnetic spectrum in order of increasing frequency.
questions.modelAnswer: Radio, microwaves, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-rays, gamma rays.
markingPoints: Radio, microwaves, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-rays, gamma rays.

questions.subtopic: 6.2 Electromagnetic waves
questions.sourceSubtopic: 6.2 Electromagnetic waves
questions.question: State three properties shared by all electromagnetic waves.
questions.modelAnswer: They are transverse. Travel at the same speed in a vacuum (3.0 × 10⁸ m/s) Can travel through a vacuum. Transfer energy.
markingPoints: Travel at the same speed in a vacuum (3.0 × 10⁸ m/s)

questions.subtopic: 6.2 Electromagnetic waves
questions.sourceSubtopic: 6.2 Electromagnetic waves
questions.question: Match radio, microwave, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-ray and gamma radiation to one common use each.
questions.modelAnswer: Radio: broadcasting/communications. Microwave: satellite/mobile communications or cooking. Infrared: heaters/thermal imaging. Visible: vision/fibre optics. UV: fluorescent lamps/security marking. X-rays: medical imaging. Gamma: sterilisation or cancer treatment.

questions.subtopic: 6.2 Electromagnetic waves
questions.sourceSubtopic: 6.2 Electromagnetic waves
questions.question: Explain the main hazards of infrared, ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays.
questions.modelAnswer: Infrared heats tissue and can burn. UV damages skin cells and eyes, causing ageing/cancer. X-rays and gamma are ionising, can damage DNA, cause mutations and cancer. Risk rises with dose.
markingPoints: Infrared heats tissue and can burn.
UV damages skin cells and eyes, causing ageing/cancer.
X-rays and gamma are ionising, can damage DNA, cause mutations and cancer.

questions.subtopic: 6.2 Electromagnetic waves
questions.sourceSubtopic: 6.2 Electromagnetic waves
questions.question: Explain why long-wavelength radio waves can be received beyond the horizon.
questions.modelAnswer: They can diffract around large obstacles and may be reflected by the ionosphere. This allows signals to travel beyond line of sight.
markingPoints: They can diffract around large obstacles and may be reflected by the ionosphere.
This allows signals to travel beyond line of sight.

questions.subtopic: 6.3 Black-body radiation
questions.sourceSubtopic: 6.3 Black-body radiation
questions.question: Define a perfect black body.
questions.modelAnswer: An object that absorbs all incident electromagnetic radiation and is the best possible emitter at a given temperature.
markingPoints: An object that absorbs all incident electromagnetic radiation and is the best possible emitter at a given temperature.

questions.subtopic: 6.3 Black-body radiation
questions.sourceSubtopic: 6.3 Black-body radiation
questions.question: Describe how a black-body radiation curve changes as temperature increases.
questions.modelAnswer: Intensity at every wavelength increases. Total emitted power increases. The peak becomes higher. Peak wavelength shifts to shorter wavelengths.
markingPoints: Peak wavelength shifts to shorter wavelengths.

questions.subtopic: 6.3 Black-body radiation
questions.sourceSubtopic: 6.3 Black-body radiation
questions.question: Explain how absorption and emission of radiation determine Earth’s temperature.
questions.modelAnswer: Earth absorbs mainly short-wave solar radiation and emits infrared. Temperature is stable when absorbed power equals emitted power. If absorption exceeds emission, temperature rises until balance is restored.
markingPoints: Earth absorbs mainly short-wave solar radiation and emits infrared.
Temperature is stable when absorbed power equals emitted power.
If absorption exceeds emission, temperature rises until balance is restored.

questions.question: Describe how to determine wave speed using a ripple tank.
questions.modelAnswer: Use a signal generator to produce steady waves. Measure frequency from the generator. Use a strobe if needed. Measure a long distance spanning several wavelengths and divide by number of wavelengths. Repeat and calculate mean wavelength. Calculate v = fλ. Keep water depth constant and view from directly above.
markingPoints: Use a signal generator to produce steady waves.
Measure a long distance spanning several wavelengths and divide by number of wavelengths.
Keep water depth constant and view from directly above.

questions.sourceSubtopic: 6.1 Waves in air, fluids and solids
questions.question: Describe how to investigate reflection and refraction of light using a ray box.
questions.modelAnswer: Place a block on paper and trace its outline. Direct a narrow ray at a marked point, mark incident/emergent rays and draw the normal. Measure angles from the normal with a protractor. Repeat for several incidence angles. Keep the same medium and entry point. Use thin precise lines.
markingPoints: Place a block on paper and trace its outline.
Direct a narrow ray at a marked point, mark incident/emergent rays and draw the normal.
Measure angles from the normal with a protractor.
Keep the same medium and entry point.
